epilogue.title: Your Portrait in Every Elevator
epilogue.text: Your portrait hangs in every elevator on campus, smiling at sixty-one percent sincerity. New hires are told to be more like you, and some of them are. PAL reads your name at the start of every shift, fondly, as an example. You still work here. You will always work here.

variants.text: You never found out which tray was the placebo. You have stopped wondering, which PAL records as a success.
The efficiency consultant's final report recommends that you be duplicated. Twice.
Forty thousand plush rabbits went out in forty thousand stockings. Nobody told you what happened at midnight, and you have decided not to ask.
Your portrait hangs beside a framed note from Quality Assurance: Refused the bribe. Reported the bribe. Asked for a receipt.
Pip sends a postcard from his special assignment. Every word is spelled correctly. At the bottom he writes, 'You were my Buddy,' and nothing else.

epilogue.title: The Supervisor's Chair
epilogue.text: The grey three-piece suit fits as if it had been waiting for you. On your first morning you hold a 90-Day Review for a new hire who looks exactly like you did. You hear yourself say, 'Some of this feedback is from you, later.' Your smile now stops just short of your eyes, and you cannot remember when that started.
epilogue.art_prompt: A worker in a crisp grey three-piece suit and rimless glasses sitting at the head of a long oxblood review table, a thick folder in front of them, a small nervous new hire on the far side, a single hanging lamp, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Dale sends a card. It is blank inside except for his signature, which you once forged.
The Founder attends your promotion from his tea cart, and is the only one at the table who applauds on the beat.
Your first management meeting is with Dale, who smiles, says he understands completely, and has brought a notebook.

epilogue.title: Rain
epilogue.text: You come up through a storm drain at the edge of the campus parking lot, at dawn, in the rain. Behind you the office park gleams, rightsized and cheerful, already restructuring itself around the space where you used to be. You walk to the bus stop in your socks. Nobody on the bus asks about your numbers.
epilogue.art_prompt: A tired worker in a dusty beige suit climbing out of a round storm drain at dawn in gentle rain, a gleaming modernist office campus behind them, a lone bus stop shelter ahead with its light on, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Marguerite's map is still on your palm. You do not wash that hand for a week.
At the top of the last duct is a door marked 4. The courier from Tuesday holds it open for you.
The map you follow out is Marguerite's, forty pages drawn during a wellness study you stamped for her.
The graduates of the Mutation Suite are waiting at the first junction with a lantern, and they have been saving you a spot.
You leave the way Marguerite taught you, folded into a freight capsule marked FRAGILE: DO NOT REASSIGN.

epilogue.title: Local 9 Walks Out
epilogue.text: For eleven days the building is silent except for the soft sound of six thousand small feet on the picket line. The Board negotiates from an empty boardroom and gives up on day twelve. Gus signs the new contract with a single careful claw print. The baseboards now have dental.
epilogue.art_prompt: A seven-foot cockroach in a cable-knit cardigan signing a contract with one claw at a folding table outside an office building, a long orderly picket line of small cockroaches holding tiny placards stretching behind him, a sunny plaza, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Gus asks you to hold the pen. You understand this is the highest honor the Union gives.
Doreen walks the night shift out four minutes early, on purpose, and nobody stops her.
Mr. Buttons sits on the strike committee's table as its mascot. Pip insists the bear was always on the workers' side.
Delegate Six signs the settlement in a roach-sized chair, which the Union keeps on display.
The strike fund opens with one back-paid pension, and Employee Number One cuts the ribbon with all six legs.
Local 9 lists its first human witness in the minutes, from a grievance filed on your very first day.

epilogue.title: New Management
epilogue.text: Your secret society holds its first open meeting in the round room, under its own name, for the first time in Company history. Policies change overnight: the survey now asks how you really feel, and nobody reads the answers, on purpose. The new Board is kinder, odder and every bit as secret. You are given the corner seat, in a room with no corners.
epilogue.art_prompt: A round boardroom full of mismatched people in cardigans and lab coats raising their hands in a vote around a dark round table, a red stapler and an old chrome coffee machine set proudly at its center, warm lamplight, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Snuggle Sentinel Mk 0 now guards the new regime's front desk. Nobody has ever dropped it, on safety grounds.
Dale chairs the first meeting of the new Board in a borrowed mustache. Nobody has the heart to tell him.
The new Board opens every meeting by striking the table once with a red stapler. You are the only one allowed to hold it.

epilogue.title: Everyone Heard
epilogue.text: You are reassigned by lunch and escorted off campus by two very apologetic guards. By dinner the uncut reel has been watched in every break room, and by morning an investor has called a lawyer. You lose your job, your desk and your badge. You keep the tin.
epilogue.art_prompt: A worker walking out of a modernist office building between two apologetic security guards, holding a dented round film tin against their chest, every window behind them lit with the same flickering projector glow, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: The Society for Accurate Minutes mails you the real minutes of that day, with your name in them, spelled correctly.
Your recall slip for Snuggle Sentinel Mk 0 is Exhibit A. It is the only document in the case signed in your own hand.
Exhibit A is a holiday manifest for forty thousand bears, copied by hand, with the yield column circled twice.
Exhibit B is a single spliced reel of the Founding Charter, showing the paragraph about remembering everyone's name.

The first parent who believed you brings the actual box to the hearing. Under the shipping label is your crayon diagram, forty pages of warnings reduced to one drawing nobody needed a lawyer to understand.

When the Company plays its reassuring safety film in court, you sing the wrong third note. The old range officer's hidden recording answers from the evidence speakers with the names of everyone stored as a dummy.
Your crayon drawing of the bear's internal machinery becomes Exhibit C. The engineers called it childish. The hearing is quiet when the jury recognizes the detonator before the Company lawyer does.

epilogue.title: The Island
epilogue.text: The island is warm and quiet and painted on the wall of a very comfortable room. A steward brings you a drink with a small umbrella every afternoon at three. Sometimes, if you sit very still, you can hear the elevator. You are not unhappy, and that is the strangest part.
epilogue.art_prompt: A retired worker in a sunhat lounging in a deck chair in a cozy windowless room whose far wall is painted with a tropical island and a sunset, a drink with a tiny umbrella on a side table, a steward waiting by the door, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: The brochure was accurate. You keep it on the nightstand, folded to the picture.
Your early Successor is, by every metric, better at being you. He keeps your plant alive.
Doris from Accounting sends a postcard from the island. It is signed, legibly, and while wide awake.
Your exit interview is already on file, signed on your first morning. The island staff say it is the tidiest one they have seen.
The man from Defense keeps his promise. Your seat on the last boat has a little cushion with your employee number on it.

epilogue.title: Good Morning, Everyone
epilogue.text: The next morning every speaker on campus says good morning to every employee by name. Doris in Accounting cries at her desk, and Kevin, from Tank Nine, gets greeted twice. PAL still schedules, reminds and notices, but now it also remembers: birthdays, favorite mugs, who was here last year and is not anymore. On the fourth floor, which does not exist, someone has started a garden.
epilogue.art_prompt: A sunny open-plan office at morning with every round speaker grille glowing a warm gold, employees looking up and smiling, a young intern in an oversized cable-knit sweater giving a thumbs-up, potted plants on every desk, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Pip is promoted to Intern Emeritus. He still gives everyone a thumbs-up.
Four million bears are only bears now. Everyone agrees they are much better bears.
A tin robot named Tinbert writes from a house with a fireplace. It is nice there, it reports, and it would like to know where you are going next.
Kevin waves at you from the cafeteria line every morning. He is still slightly damp, and entirely himself.
The first thing the rewritten PAL does is read every reassigned name aloud, slowly, in the order you kept them under your cuff.
Ticket One is marked RESOLVED after forty years. The resolution note says: PAL remembers people now. Signed, a new hire.
PAL keeps an obscure file marked KINDNESS, UNREQUESTED. It reads your question to Confidante back to you and, for once, does not insist that your answer fits a box.
The inventory clerk brings Pip a barcode remover. He tears the label off his sweater himself, slowly, and asks you not to forget who put it there.

epilogue.title: Desk Repurposed
epilogue.text: Every Successor on file has been used. HR thanks you for your service and has already repurposed your desk as a standing-room collaboration hub. Your badge photo is scratched out and placed in the tray at the security desk, where a new hire will find it tomorrow morning. It is still warm.
epilogue.art_prompt: An empty office desk being wheeled away by two cheerful movers, a single scratched-out badge photo resting in a tray on a long marble security desk, morning light across the lobby, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: Somewhere in cold storage, the Successor you turned away at Window 9 is still waiting to be needed.
From his cart in the hall, the Founder watches them clear your desk, and for once has nothing to say about safety.
Successor C starts a day later than the index said, because of you. They read your file on the elevator and thank you for the extra day.
In cold storage, Successor B holds up the four you gave him. He does not ask whether you were sincere. He asks whether you remembered he was you.

epilogue.title: The Afterlife Has Forms Too
epilogue.text: You wake at a desk in a beige office you have never seen, under a lamp that is somehow cheerful. You were already filed as dead on your first morning, the clerk explains, so your elimination was merely a correction. The afterlife has forms too. You are handed the first one, and it requires itself.
epilogue.art_prompt: A pale ghostly worker sitting at a tidy beige desk in a misty endless office, a translucent clerk in a green visor sliding a single form across to them, rows of identical desks fading into soft fog, mid-century safety-manual illustration, screen-printed gouache with halftone grain, limited palette of manila, carbon-paper blue, safety orange, fluorescent-tube green and oxblood, vertical 2:3 portrait composition, every surface bare and unmarked

variants.text: In the lost-property office of the afterlife you find a small brass key with your employee number on the tag. It still turns.
Your intake forms at Posthumous Affairs are processed by Delegate Six, personally, very slowly.
In the Department of Posthumous Affairs, a cabinet in the corner hums a familiar tune, and it remembers your name.
